structure.title: Mowgli's world
structure.text: Stories about the human child establish the jungle's laws, teachers, enemies, and competing forms of belonging.

structure.title: Other animal societies
structure.text: Separate tales and poems move beyond Mowgli, testing courage, intelligence, and cooperation in different settings.

people.name: Mowgli
people.text: A small boy who wanders into a wolf family's cave as a baby and is raised in the jungle, learning its law from his teachers.

people.name: Baloo and Bagheera
people.text: The old brown bear who teaches Mowgli the laws and languages of the jungle, and the black panther who bought his life with a bull.

people.name: Shere Khan
people.text: The lame tiger who claims Mowgli as his rightful prey and never stops waiting for the wolves to give him up.

context.title: A collection
context.text: The book is not one uninterrupted Mowgli adventure. Other stories develop related concerns through different animals and human encounters.
context.takeaway: Let each tale establish its own world.

context.title: Law and hierarchy
context.text: Animal societies distribute rank and obligations. Their arrangements invite attention to who makes rules and who benefits from them.
context.takeaway: Order is a subject, not just a background.

notice.why: Survival depends on learned social knowledge.

notice.text: Compare individual courage with help from others.
notice.why: Clever cooperation often matters as much as strength.

opening: Mowgli grows up among wolves, learning rules that can keep him alive among creatures capable of killing him. Belonging requires more than affection: the jungle has debts, councils, enemies, and punishments, and the tiger has never accepted his place in it. Around Mowgli's adventures, Kipling tells other stories of animals facing danger with courage, cunning, and unlikely allies. The pleasure comes from entering societies with their own customs and voices, where a human child may need considerable education before he can behave intelligently.
